nameStory: The harlequin duck gets its colorful name from Harlequin, a flamboyantly dressed character in Italian comedy theater who wore a patchwork costume of bright, contrasting colors. Just like that theatrical character, the male duck sports a stunning array of white stripes and patches against deep blue-gray plumage that looks almost costume-like. The scientific name 'histrionicus' also means 'actor' in Latin, doubling down on this theatrical theme!
description: The harlequin duck is a small, compact sea duck that's like a living work of art bobbing on the waves. Males are absolutely stunning with their intricate pattern of white stripes and spots on slate-blue and chestnut plumage, while females are a more subdued brown with white patches around the face. They're smaller than most ducks you'll see, roughly the size of a large pigeon, with a rounded head and relatively short bill perfect for their rugged coastal lifestyle.

idTips.label: Male breeding plumage
idTips.description: Males have an unmistakable bold pattern of white stripes and round spots against deep slate-blue and rusty-brown feathers - like someone painted racing stripes on a duck

idTips.label: Female markings
idTips.description: Females are chocolate-brown overall with distinctive white patches around the face, including a white spot behind the eye that stands out even from a distance

idTips.label: Body shape and size
idTips.description: Compact and chunky with a rounded head and short neck - they sit low and tight on the water like a cork, much smaller than mallards

idTips.label: Behavior in water
idTips.description: They dive frequently and seem to disappear underwater for long periods, often popping up far from where they went down

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Fly fast and low over the water in tight groups, with rapid wingbeats that create a whirring sound you can hear as they pass

idTips.label: Voice
idTips.description: Males make distinctive mouse-like squeaking calls, earning them the nickname 'squeaker' - quite different from typical duck quacks

habitat: Along New England's rocky coastlines, especially where waves crash against granite ledges and kelp forests grow in the shallow waters. They prefer areas with strong currents and plenty of underwater rocks where they can dive for shellfish, sea urchins, and small crabs. You'll often spot them around jetties, breakwaters, and the surf zones of exposed headlands from Maine down through Massachusetts.

seasonality.spring: Males are in their most spectacular breeding plumage, making identification easy as they begin pairing up along the coast before heading north to breed.
seasonality.summer: Most have departed for Arctic breeding grounds, though a few non-breeding birds may linger along the Maine coast looking somewhat disheveled in molting plumage.
seasonality.fall: They begin returning in late fall, with males still showing remnants of their breeding colors mixed with duller winter feathers.
seasonality.winter: Peak viewing time when flocks gather along New England's coast, though males are in subdued winter plumage that's less dramatically patterned but still distinctive.

funFact: Harlequin ducks are such skilled divers that they can swim underwater against powerful ocean currents to pluck shellfish directly off wave-battered rocks - they're essentially the underwater acrobats of the duck world, performing aquatic stunts that would challenge a seal!
confusionNotes: Female harlequins might be confused with female surf scoters, but harlequins are much smaller and have those distinctive white face patches, while female scoters are larger and more uniformly dark. Remember: harlequins have the white 'headlights' on their face that scoters lack.
contextualKnowledge: Despite their many colorful nicknames like 'totem pole duck' and 'painted duck,' they're also called 'lords and ladies' - a charming reference to how the elaborately dressed males seem to court the more modestly attired females, like fancy aristocrats at a ball.
compareHints: Harlequin ducks are the only species in their genus, making them unique among North American ducks. Compared to other small sea ducks like bufflehead, harlequins are less contrasting in their patterns (no pure black and white) and prefer rougher, rockier waters rather than calmer bays. Unlike the diving ducks they're often grouped with, harlequins have that distinctive theatrical costume appearance rather than the bold black-and-white patterns of scoters or the clean geometric patterns of goldeneyes.
